title: The smith and the silver (239–243)
hook: as a smith removes impurities from silver, little by little; ignorance the greatest taint

segments.voice: Yesterday, dīpa: at the door of the journey, make yourself an island. Your line was make an island.

Take out an old silver spoon, the kind that sat in a drawer for years. It's gone dark, almost black in places. Rub it with a soft cloth and a little polish, and at first nothing happens. Then a faint gleam appears at the edge of the bowl. Rub more, and a little more of it comes back. You can't polish the whole spoon in one stroke. But stroke by stroke, the silver was there all along. Chapter eighteen of the Dhammapada puts a silversmith right in the middle of its teaching.
screen: `A TARNISHED SILVER SPOON.` → `A FAINT GLEAM AT THE EDGE.` → `THE SILVER WAS THERE ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Verse two thirty-nine, in Max Müller's translation: "Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time." Picture an ancient smith at the furnace, melting silver and blowing the dross off the top, not all of it in one breath. The chapter's name is Malavagga, and mala means a stain, a taint, the dross. The old commentary tells of a brahmin who noticed monks' robes getting wet from dew as they walked through long grass, so he cleared the grass. Later he saw them getting dusty, so he spread sand. Then he built a shelter against the sun and rain. One small thing at a time, never a grand plan, and the Buddha praised him with this verse. Then the chapter lists taints, the way a household list would. Verse two forty-one: "The taint of prayers is non-repetition; the taint of houses, non-repair". A chant you stop reciting fades from memory. A house you stop mending falls apart. Neglect is its own kind of stain. Then the heaviest line, verse two forty-three: "But there is a taint worse than all taints,--ignorance is the greatest taint." Ignorance, avijjā, isn't about not knowing facts. It's not seeing how things really are: that they change, that craving hurts. The verse calls it worse than all the rest, and ends by telling the monks to throw it off. Which is why the polishing never stops. The silver is there.
screen: `THE SMITH BLOWS OFF THE DROSS.` · `A BRAHMIN, ONE SMALL THING AT A TIME.` · `NEGLECT IS A STAIN.` · `IGNORANCE, THE GREATEST TAINT.` · then, large: `LITTLE BY LITTLE.`

segments.voice: If you can, pick up something small that needs care, a spoon, your glasses, a mug with a stain, or picture one, and slowly wipe it, just a little, noticing the small change. Then close your eyes and do the same with the mind: with each out-breath, let one small speck of irritation or worry blow off the top, like dross from silver. Not all of it; one by one, little by little.
Mala. A stain, a taint, the dross: verse two thirty-nine says as a smith blows the impurities off silver, one by one, little by little, the wise clear their own.
Your line: little by little. One by one, and from time to time. On we go.

howItsDone: Buddhist practice is often described as gradual purification, and teachers use the smith and the silver to encourage steady daily effort rather than dramatic change.

original.note: Pali: stain, taint, impurity — chapter eighteen is the Malavagga; avijjā paramaṃ malaṃ, ignorance is the greatest taint.

trapdoor: what you thought: get rid of your flaws.
what it means: clear them like a smith clears silver, one by one, little by little; the silver was there all along.
what a scholar hears: avijjā, ignorance, is the root taint and the first link of dependent origination; Müller's 'taint of prayers' renders the neglect of recitation.
recall: an island, and also a lamp
a steady happiness and ease of mind

chat.says: I've tried to change for years and still slip up. Am I just failing at this?
options: The verse says clear faults like a smith clears silver: one by one, little by little.
The verse says real change happens all at once, so years of slips mean you're failing.
The verse says some people have no silver in them, so polishing will never help.
chat.meaning: Verse 239: as a smith blows the dross off silver, one by one, little by little, the wise clear their own. The polishing never stops; the silver is there.
